To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the nutritional requirements of a normal subject increase with physical activity and that they remain high for a long time in patients with denutrtion.

(a) physical exercise, even at a low level of intensity, increases both the rate and efficiency of protein-energy metabolism; (b) this is true for all forms of physical activity; (c) the increase in protein-energy metabolism is proportional to the intensity of physical activity; and (d) this increase in protein-energy expenditure is not limited to the period of exercise itself, but is sustained for a period of time after exercise.
physical activity increases protein synthesis and decreases protein breakdown.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following points: 1. The relationship between energy expenditure and protein synthesis.

the following points: 1) the influence of physical activity on the nutritional requirements of normal and denutritional subjects; 2) the influence of denutrition on physical activity in normal subjects and in patients; and 3) the influence of ambulatory techniques of nutritional support on physical activity and on the nutritional status of hospitalized patients.
the following questions: (1) What are the consequences of physical activity on the metabolism of proteins and amino-acids?

(1) physical activity has a direct effect on protein synthesis and breakdown, and on protein turnover, (2) protein synthesis and breakdown are affected differently by physical activity, and that protein breakdown is more affected than protein synthesis, (3) physical activity has an indirect effect on protein synthesis by increasing the availability of amino acids, and (4) physical activity has no significant effect on protein requirements.

physical activity and protein-energy metabolism are intimately linked and that the nutritional requirements of a patient depend not only on the severity and duration of the disease, but also on the degree and nature of physical exertion, as well as the patient's age.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for a given patient, the more active he or she is, the more protein and energy he/she needs.

(a) physical activity is an essential factor in determining nutritional requirements, (b) physical activity is a factor which must be taken into account when calculating the protein requirements of hospitalized patients, and (c) physical activity is one of the most important factors determining the success of enteral or parental nutrition in hospitalized patients.
the relationship between physical activity and nutritional requirements is a very complex one and is still far from being understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to avoid the deleterious effects of immobilization, it is necessary to maintain the physical activity of patients, even if they are bedridden.
the use of non-ambulatory nutrition support techniques is a major cause of the metabolic disorders and complications that occur in patients with denutritional disorders.
physical activity, and especially the ability to move about, is an essential factor in determining protein-energy metabolism.
